summary: Specifies how DNS resource records are named and structured so clients can discover services. Given a service type and a domain, a client can find a list of named instances of that service using standard DNS queries. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like looking up printers in a phone book. You ask the book for printers in this building and it gives you a list of names you can pick from.

subtitle: How ordinary DNS records can list the printers, web pages and other services on a network, with no new DNS features.

tldr.problem: Clients need to find which instances of a kind of service exist in a domain, pick one by a friendly name, and then learn where to connect, without every site adopting a new discovery system.
tldr.mechanism: A PTR query for a service type and domain returns the names of service instances. Each instance name has an SRV record giving host and port, and a TXT record carrying key/value details.
tldr.outcome: The same records work over Multicast DNS for zero configuration on a local link and over conventional unicast DNS for larger sites. RFC 6763 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 6763 is a Proposed Standard and is listed as updated by RFC 8553; it has not been obsoleted. The RFC itself notes it is designed to run over Multicast DNS (RFC 6762) as well as ordinary unicast DNS.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Goals
sections.content:
RFC 6763 specifies how DNS resource records are named and structured so that clients can discover services. This mechanism is called DNS-based Service Discovery, or DNS-SD. Given a type of service and a domain, a client gets a list of named instances of that service using standard DNS queries.

The document proposes no change to the structure of DNS messages and defines no new operation codes, response codes or record types. It builds on the DNS SRV record from RFC 2782 and the TXT record from RFC 1035, and it works with both Multicast DNS (RFC 6762) and existing unicast DNS software.

Three design goals are named. A client must be able to list the instances of a service type in a domain (browsing). Given one instance name, it must be able to resolve it efficiently to an address and port. And instance names should stay relatively persistent, so a printer chosen today can still be used tomorrow even if its address or port changed. The protocol should also be simple enough that any IP-capable device can implement it.

With Multicast DNS, a device's services are advertised on the local link with no further user interaction. With conventional unicast DNS, some configuration, such as the domain to register in and DNS Update keys, is usually needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to reuse the phone book everyone already has, DNS, instead of building a new one. You can find things by type, pick one by name, and it still works tomorrow even if the thing moved.

sections.title: Service Instance Names and Browsing
sections.content:
Traditional SRV lookups suit services whose instances are interchangeable, such as identical web servers. They do not suit printers, where picking one at random is probably not what the user wanted. DNS-SD adds one level of indirection: the client asks for PTR records with the name <Service>.<Domain>, and gets back zero or more Service Instance Names of the form <Instance>.<Service>.<Domain>.

The Instance part is a user-friendly name in Net-Unicode text. It MUST NOT contain ASCII control characters but may contain spaces, dots, accented characters and non-Roman text. It is stored as a single DNS label of UTF-8, so it is limited to 63 octets. The Service part is two labels: an underscore plus the service name, then _tcp for TCP applications or _udp for all others. The Domain may be local. for link-local Multicast DNS or an ordinary unicast domain.

Clients usually show only the first label to the user. Because the Instance part can contain dots, software that joins the three parts into one string MUST preserve label boundaries; the RFC recommends escaping a literal dot as \. and a backslash as \\.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for printers gives you a list of friendly names like Front Desk Printer. You choose by name, not by a string of numbers.

sections.title: Resolving an Instance to a Host and Port
sections.content:
Once a user picks a name, the client queries for the SRV and TXT records of that Service Instance Name. The SRV record gives the target host name and port number. The TXT record gives extra details, described in the next section.

The RFC points out that SRV records remove the need for preassigned port numbers. Only 65535 TCP port numbers exist and they are normally allocated one per application protocol, so most ports on any given host go unused for its whole life. With SRV, each host can allocate ports dynamically to the services it actually runs and advertise them.

If several SRV records come back, clients MUST honor priority and weight: lower-numbered priority is preferred, and servers of equal priority are chosen randomly in proportion to weight. In the common case of one SRV record per instance, priority and weight SHOULD both be zero.
sections.plainLanguage: After you pick a name, DNS tells you which computer to go to and which door number to knock on.

sections.title: TXT Record Key/Value Data
sections.content:
Every DNS-SD service MUST have a TXT record with the same name as its SRV record, even if there is nothing to store and the TXT record is just a single zero byte. This lets the service control the TTL of that record instead of falling back to the negative caching TTL. Implementations MUST NOT emit a TXT record with zero strings.

A TXT record is a series of strings, each a length byte followed by 0 to 255 bytes. DNS-SD stores one key=value pair per string. Everything up to the first = is the key, and the rest, including later = signs, is the value. A string with no = is a boolean attribute that is simply present. Unknown keys MUST be silently ignored, and the host and port MUST NOT be repeated in the TXT record.

Keys must be printable US-ASCII except =, are case-insensitive, and SHOULD be no more than nine characters long. A key SHOULD NOT appear twice, and if it does the client MUST use only the first occurrence. Values are opaque binary data. A typical record is meant to be 200 bytes or less, under 400 bytes should fit one 512-byte DNS message, under 1300 bytes should fit one 1500-byte Ethernet packet, and anything larger is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Profile authors are advised to include txtvers=x as the first pair, so clients can ignore TXT formats they do not understand. Ideally it stays at txtvers=1 forever, with improvements added as new keys that older clients ignore.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra details are written as little labeled notes, like paper=A4. A client reads the notes it understands and ignores the rest.

sections.title: Service Names and Subtypes
sections.content:
The service name identifies both what a service does and which protocol it speaks. Names follow the IANA rules from RFC 6335: at most fifteen characters, only letters, digits and hyphens, no consecutive hyphens, and at least one letter. Case is ignored. The name should reflect the real service, not just the protocol it borrows. For example, iTunes music sharing is built on HTTP GET but advertises _daap._tcp rather than _http._tcp, so it does not appear in ordinary web browsers.

For narrowing results, DNS-SD offers subtypes. A printer's embedded web page can be advertised under _http._tcp and also under the _printer subtype. A printer-management tool then queries _printer._sub._http._tcp.<Domain> to see only those pages. Both PTR records point to the same SRV and TXT pair, so the instance name does not change. The RFC says subtypes fit only when some clients want the whole set and others want a subset.

The 15-character limit exists because a fully qualified name may be up to 255 bytes, and the service domain and parent domain must also fit. The RFC works through the budget and concludes that parent domains of 100 bytes or less leave DNS-SD fully usable. It also notes that a single unicast response can list up to 839 instances with maximum-sized instance names, and that more than 100 instances in a flat list is probably too many for a user, so large networks should be divided into logical subdomains.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of service gets a short name tag. You can also add a special sticker, like printer, so people who only want printers can skip everything else.

sections.title: Flagship Naming and Service Type Enumeration
sections.content:
Many printers speak several printing protocols, such as LPR, IPP and a raw page-description stream on TCP port 9100. A client that knows more than one can browse for all of them, merge the results into one list and suppress duplicate names. The risk is that two different printers could both be named Sales Department just because they implement different protocols.

To prevent this, one protocol in a family is declared the flagship, typically the oldest or best known. A device that does not implement the flagship protocol creates a placeholder SRV record with that name (priority 0, weight 0, port 0, target set to its own host name). If a record already exists, the name is taken and the device must pick another. No PTR record is created for the placeholder, so it is not discoverable. With Multicast DNS, the target MUST NOT be the empty root label, or conflicts would go undetected.

For diagnosis and management tools there is also a meta-query: a PTR query for _services._dns-sd._udp.<Domain> returns the service types advertised in that domain.
sections.plainLanguage: If two printers both want to be called Sales Department, a shared sign-up sheet keeps one of them from taking the same name.

sections.title: Populating DNS and Discovering Domains
sections.content:
How the PTR, SRV and TXT records get into DNS is outside the scope of the RFC. It lists examples: an administrator editing the name server configuration, a tool that writes a zone file, a printer manager that uses DNS Update or answers queries for a delegated subdomain, printers that register themselves with Dynamic DNS Update, and Zeroconf printers that answer Multicast DNS queries under local..

A visiting laptop or phone should also find browsing and registration domains without manual setup. Five reserved names are queried with PTR: b, db, r, dr and lb, each under _dns-sd._udp.<domain>. They return, in order, domains recommended for browsing, a default browsing domain, domains for registering, a default registration domain, and the legacy or automatic browsing domains. These answers are purely advisory.

The domain can be local., can come from DHCP options or IPv6 Router Advertisements, or can be derived from the host's own address and subnet mask via the reverse-mapping name. Servers SHOULD also add related records to responses. A PTR answer SHOULD carry the SRV and TXT records it names plus the A and AAAA records for the SRV target, but clients MUST still work if these extras are missing.
sections.plainLanguage: When you walk into a new building, your device can ask the network which phone books to look in, and the network points the way.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
DNS-SD is only a convention for naming and using existing DNS records, so it adds no security requirements beyond those already applying to DNS queries and updates. The RFC says DNSSEC should be used where authenticity of query results matters, and secure DNS updates should generally control which clients may change records. It also reminds clients that they decide whether to trust additional records in a response.

For IANA, the registry of service names is the one managed under RFC 6335. When a protocol uses subtypes, they should be documented in its specification or the notes field of the registration. When a protocol belongs to a family with a flagship, the registrant should record the flagship name in the notes field. For example, the registrations for ipp and pdl-datastream reference printer as the flagship.
sections.plainLanguage: It does not add new locks. If you need to be sure the answers are real, use the locks DNS already has.
